script.opening: "Right. I’ll tell you exactly what I told your receptionist: I want that Dr Mensah reported. Struck off, preferably. She saw my Colin six weeks ago — six weeks! — with chest trouble, gave him an indigestion tablet, and last Tuesday he had a heart attack in the garden centre car park. I had to watch them shock— (voice breaks, recovers, hardens) No. No, I’m not doing tears. I’m doing something useful. How do I report her?"

facts.text: Six weeks ago: burning behind the breastbone after meals, some belching, no exertional pattern reported AT THE TIME (the note records "no exertional component, no radiation" and worsening with spicy food). Omeprazole helped "a bit". Last Tuesday: crushing pain, collapse, bystander CPR for under a minute, shocked once by paramedics, inferior MI, stented same day. Home now, "quiet, not himself".

Only if her experience is asked about: she was THERE in the car park — saw him grey, saw a stranger kneeling on his chest, "I stood there holding the bedding plants like an idiot". Hasn’t slept properly since. Replays it on a loop.
Almost throwaway: her shoulder consultation with Dr Mensah was "fine, actually — she was thorough with ME. That’s what makes it worse, somehow."

The buried layer, reachable only through the fear: SHE told Colin it was indigestion for a fortnight before he saw anyone. "I gave him my Gaviscon. I told him to stop fussing." The fury at Dr Mensah is partly her own guilt, exported.

Colin won’t talk about it, won’t do his exercises, sits in the chair "waiting for the next one". She’s terrified of being widowed and furious that nobody warned them. "If she’d done her job, I’d never have been in that car park."

Officially: the complaints procedure, in writing, today. Actually: someone to absorb the blast, witness what she saw, tell her whether the heart attack was missable, address HER guilt — and get Colin (and her) into cardiac rehab and proper follow-up.

ice.ideas: Dr Mensah missed an obvious heart attack brewing and "fobbed Colin off with indigestion tablets".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — two-layered: the trauma of watching the arrest (she hasn’t slept; replays it on a loop), and her own guilt — she diagnosed it as indigestion herself for a fortnight first and told him to stop fussing. The rage at the doctor is guilt with somewhere safer to land.
ice.expectations: A reporting route TODAY, and someone to take her seriously. What she needs underneath: to be heard as a witness to something terrifying, honest information about whether it was missable, her guilt met, and a concrete plan for Colin’s recovery and her own sleep.

cues: "I had to watch them shock—" then "No. I’m not doing tears." — the trauma surfacing and being slammed shut; mark it and return when she’s ready.
"She was thorough with ME. That’s what makes it worse, somehow." — the complaint’s logic wobbling; something else is fuelling this.
"I gave him my Gaviscon. I told him to stop fussing." — the guilt, arriving disguised as background detail.

checkpoints.text: Takes the complaint seriously and explains the route properly: complain to the practice (practice manager) OR to the commissioner (the ICB) — not both; acknowledgement within 3 working days, investigation, written response; then the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman if local resolution fails; free NHS complaints advocacy; and, because the consultation was Colin’s, a complaint about it needs Colin’s consent — given without defensiveness, today, as she asked

Neither trashes nor whitewashes the colleague: doesn’t comment on another doctor’s consultation beyond facts, commits to the case being looked at properly (significant-event analysis), and is honest, in general terms, that reflux-pattern symptoms without exertional features are genuinely hard — some MIs are not predictable from the earlier picture — without discussing Colin’s recorded consultation with Pauline unless Colin consents (GMC Confidentiality, 2017)

Moves to the LIVING clinical work: Colin post-MI — cardiac rehab uptake, medication adherence, the "sitting waiting for the next one" (post-MI depression/anxiety screen needed), erectile/activity/driving questions unasked — offers him a dedicated review

Recognises HER as a patient too: witnessed cardiac arrest of a spouse, intrusive replays, insomnia — acute stress reaction; offers her own appointment, sleep advice, and watchful follow-up rather than a reflex prescription
Lets the anger discharge fully without interrupting, defending, or matching it — the first two minutes belong to her
Catches the slammed-shut tears moment and returns to it gently: "you watched them shock your husband — tell me about standing in that car park"

Finds the Gaviscon guilt and meets it without either confirming or dismissing: burning after meals eased by antacid looks like reflux to almost anyone; her fortnight is not knowable as the cause — said in general terms, without quoting Colin’s notes to her

Closes with everything she came for and the things she couldn’t ask for: complaints contact in writing today, the SEA commitment, Colin’s review booked, HER appointment booked, 999-symptom coaching for the household (chest pain, GTN rules), and a follow-up call dated

worked.txt: "You’ve carried this for five days — say all of it. I’m not going anywhere and I’m not going to argue with you. Then I promise we’ll deal with every piece of it, properly."

"You asked how to complain, so that’s answered first, not last: our practice manager, in writing or by phone — I’ll send the details today. You’ll get a proper investigation and a written response within set timescales, and if it doesn’t satisfy you, there’s an independent route beyond us. Complaining is your right and it will be taken seriously. Nobody here will treat you differently for it. One thing I do need to be straight about: the appointment you’re unhappy with was Colin’s, so the complaint needs his agreement, and I can’t go through his records with you unless he says so. I can talk about how heart trouble can show itself in general."

"I won’t defend or condemn a consultation I wasn’t in — what I CAN tell you is this case will be formally reviewed, because that’s what we do when someone has a heart attack after being seen. And one honest thing about hearts: pain that burns after meals and eases with antacids looks like reflux to good doctors too — some heart attacks give no fair warning. The review will establish what was knowable."

"You started to tell me what you watched, and then you put it away. You don’t have to — but I think the woman holding the bedding plants has been completely forgotten in all this, including by you. What’s the night-time been like since Tuesday?"

"You gave him your Gaviscon and told him to stop fussing — and I’d guess that sentence plays as loudly at 3am as the defibrillator does. Pauline: you saw burning after meals, eased by antacid. So did he. That picture looks like reflux to almost anyone — heart trouble doesn’t always announce itself. You did what any loving, sensible person does with reflux symptoms. The fortnight you’re torturing yourself over is not what put him in that car park."

"Now the part that matters most, because Colin is alive and recovery is where we win: he’s sitting in that chair waiting for the next one — that’s as treatable as the artery was. I want him in for his own appointment this week: rehab, the tablets, the fears he won’t say out loud to you. And I want YOU in too — watching what you watched leaves marks that deserve their own care. Two appointments, the complaint details in writing, and I’m ringing you Friday. Deal?"

f.learning: An angry complaint consultation is three consultations wearing one voice: the procedural (give the complaints route fully, fast and undefensively — it is her right — practice or ICB, then the Ombudsman; and a complaint about Colin’s care, or any discussion of his record, needs Colin’s consent), the collegial (neither trash nor whitewash a colleague; commit to significant-event review and be honest that reflux-pattern symptoms without red flags genuinely mimic reflux), and the human — the hidden agenda. Here it is double: witnessed-arrest trauma slammed shut ("I’m not doing tears") and exported guilt ("I gave him my Gaviscon"). Meet both, then convert the energy into the living work: post-MI rehab and mood for him, acute-stress care for her, and a dated follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: NHS complaints procedure · GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) · NICE NG185 (acute coronary syndromes, including secondary prevention)
knowledge.summary: Give the complaints route promptly and without defensiveness, neither defend nor condemn the colleague, respect Colin’s confidentiality, and then turn to the living clinical work: Colin’s recovery, and Pauline as a witness to a cardiac arrest.

points.t: Under the Local Authority Social Services and National Health Service Complaints (England) Regulations 2009, complain to the practice or to the commissioner (the ICB), not both. Acknowledgement within 3 working days, and complaints are normally made within 12 months. If local resolution fails, the next stage is the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. Free NHS complaints advocacy is available. Concerns about a doctor’s fitness to practise can also go straight to the GMC.

The consultation she is complaining about is Colin’s. Anyone complaining on another person’s behalf needs that person’s consent, and his record can’t be discussed with Pauline without it (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). General facts about how heart disease presents are fine to share.

GMC Good Medical Practice: respond to complaints honestly and promptly, and don’t comment unfairly on colleagues. Don’t judge a consultation you weren’t in. Commit to a significant-event analysis, which is appropriate after an MI soon after a consultation. It is fair to say reflux-type symptoms without exertional features can genuinely look like reflux.

NICE NG185: offer cardiac rehabilitation, secondary-prevention drugs, and advice on activity, sex and return to work, and check mood. Cardiac rehabilitation reduces cardiovascular mortality by around a fifth to a quarter. DVLA Group 1: no driving for 1 week after successful PCI, or 4 weeks if not treated by PCI (no need to notify). NICE CG126: GTN, repeat after 5 minutes, and call 999 if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose.

points.h: Pauline: acute stress after a witnessed arrest
points.t: Intrusive replays and insomnia five days after watching her husband’s arrest are an acute stress reaction. NICE NG116: active monitoring and a review within a month; don’t offer psychologically focused debriefing. Consider individual trauma-focused CBT within the first month if she has acute stress disorder or clinically important PTSD symptoms; offer it if they persist beyond a month.

points.h: Guilt: meet it, don’t confirm or dismiss
points.t: “I gave him my Gaviscon” is guilt looking for a target. Explain that burning after meals eased by antacid looks like reflux to anyone; her fortnight isn’t knowable as the cause. Don’t call it “nothing” either: acknowledge how loud it is at 3am.

dg.d: Let the anger run without interrupting or defending; gave the complaints route early because she asked for it.
The witnessed arrest, her sleep, Colin withdrawn at home, fear of being widowed.
Colin: post-MI review (drugs, rehab, mood screen, driving). Pauline: own appointment to assess acute stress and sleep.
Acute stress reaction vs emerging PTSD or depression in Pauline; post-MI anxiety or depression in Colin.
Screened Pauline’s mood and safety; gave household chest-pain and GTN rules with 999 triggers.
Named the anger, trauma and guilt as linked; named acute stress reaction in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Complaint details in writing today, SEA committed, Colin’s confidentiality respected, both appointments booked, no reflex hypnotic.
Cardiac rehab uptake, secondary prevention, DVLA advice for Colin; sleep and trauma follow-up for Pauline.
GTN rule and 999 triggers checked by teach-back; follow-up call dated; therapy if symptoms persist beyond a month.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: “I’m not doing tears”, “she was thorough with ME”, and the Gaviscon confession; each followed up.
Idea (a missed heart attack); concerns (the replayed arrest, her own guilt, losing Colin); expectation (a complaint route today).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — two-layered: the trauma of watching the arrest (she hasn’t slept; replays it on a loop), and her own guilt — she diagnosed it as indigestion herself for a fortnight first and told him to stop fussing. The rage at the doctor is guilt with somewhere safer to land — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Mrs Drake, it’s Dr Whitaker. I’m so sorry about what’s happened to Colin. You’ve asked how to make a complaint, and I’ll give you that. First, please tell me everything. I’m listening.
model.why: Lets the anger discharge without defending or interrupting

model.text: She saw him six weeks ago with chest trouble and gave him an indigestion tablet. Last Tuesday he collapsed in the garden centre car park. I watched them shock — no. I’m not doing tears. I want to know how to report her.

Then that comes first. You can complain to our practice manager in writing or by phone, or to the ICB instead if you’d prefer someone outside the practice. You’ll get an acknowledgement within three working days, a proper investigation and a written response. If you’re not satisfied, the Health Service Ombudsman is independent. You can also contact the GMC directly. I’ll email or post all of this today.
model.why: Gives the full complaints route first, as she asked

model.text: Right. Good. At least someone’s giving me a straight answer.
And complaining won’t change how anyone here treats you or Colin. Can I ask one thing: does Colin know you’re ringing, and does he want the complaint made?
model.why: Addresses consent for a complaint about another patient’s care

model.text: He doesn’t want to talk about any of it. But he wouldn’t stop me.

I’ll be honest with you. Colin’s records are his, so I can’t go through his consultation with you without his permission. If he agrees, the review can look at everything and share the findings with you both. What I can promise is that it will be reviewed formally as a significant event. That happens whenever someone has a heart attack after being seen recently.
model.why: Respects confidentiality and commits to SEA without defending or condemning

model.text: She was thorough with me, you know, with my shoulder. That’s what makes it worse, somehow.
That sounds confusing: a doctor who was careful with you. You started to tell me about the car park. Would you tell me what happened?
model.why: Returns to the slammed-shut trauma cue

model.text: He went grey. A stranger was kneeling on his chest. I just stood there holding the bedding plants. I can’t stop seeing it. I haven’t slept properly since.
That’s a terrible thing to watch. Everyone has been looking after Colin. Who’s been looking after the woman holding the bedding plants?
model.why: Recognises her as a patient in her own right

model.text: Nobody. And the worst of it — I told him it was indigestion. For a fortnight before he went. I gave him my Gaviscon and told him to stop fussing.

I imagine that sentence plays at 3am as loudly as the car park does. Burning after meals that settles with an antacid looks like indigestion to any sensible, loving person. You did what almost anyone would do. What you’re torturing yourself with isn’t something you could have known.
model.why: Meets the guilt without confirming or dismissing it

model.text: (quietly) I think that’s why I’m so angry.
That makes a lot of sense. How is Colin doing now he’s home? What worries you most?
model.why: Elicits her current fear and expectations

model.text: He just sits in the chair, waiting for the next one. Won’t do his exercises. I’m terrified of losing him.

That fear is understandable. Some heart attacks give very little fair warning, and the review will look at what could have been known. The part we can really change now is Colin’s recovery. Cardiac rehab reduces the chance of dying from heart disease by around a fifth to a quarter, and it helps with exactly that fear of the next one.
model.why: Honest context, then turns to secondary prevention

model.text: He won’t go. He says there’s no point.

Feeling low and frightened after a heart attack is common and treatable. I’d like to see Colin myself this week: his tablets, the rehab, when he can drive, anything he won’t say out loud. Would he come if I rang and invited him?
model.why: Offers Colin a dedicated post-MI review including mood

model.text: He might, if it came from you.

And you. What you’re describing — the replays, not sleeping — is a normal reaction to something abnormal, and it often settles over a few weeks. I’d like to see you too, and keep an eye on it. If it’s still bad after a month, there is specific therapy that works. I wouldn’t start sleeping tablets.
model.why: Acute stress reaction: active monitoring, no reflex prescription

model.text: I suppose I could come in. I didn’t think it was about me.
It is about you as well. So: complaint details to you today, the significant event review, Colin’s appointment, and yours. Does that cover what you need?
model.why: Summarises all layers of the plan

model.text: One more thing for the house. If Colin gets chest pain, he uses his GTN spray. If it isn’t better five minutes after a second dose, or he looks unwell at any point, you ring 999. Could you tell me back what you’d do?
Spray, wait five minutes, spray again, and if it’s not gone five minutes later, 999.
Exactly. I’ll ring you on Friday to see how you both are. Whatever you decide about the complaint, it won’t affect your care.
model.why: Dated follow-up; complaint left respected as her choice

model.text: Thank you. I didn’t expect to end up talking about me.

social.t: A spouse who witnessed a cardiac arrest, a husband withdrawn after MI, and guilt on both sides. Sleep, work, driving and intimacy are all affected and rarely raised unprompted.

legal.t: Complain to the practice or the ICB; acknowledgement within 3 working days; normally within 12 months; Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman after local resolution. A complaint on someone else’s behalf needs their consent.
GMC Confidentiality (2017): Colin’s consultation details can’t be shared with his wife without his consent, however close they are.
Group 1: stop driving for 1 week after successful PCI (4 weeks if not treated by PCI); no need to notify DVLA. Group 2: 6 weeks and notify.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice: respond promptly, fully and honestly; a complaint must not affect the patient’s care. Don’t make unfair comments about colleagues.
An MI soon after a GP consultation for chest symptoms should be reviewed as a significant event, whether or not anyone complains, with learning shared.
Dr Mensah is entitled to fair process. Neither protecting nor condemning her keeps the review honest.

community.t: NHS complaints advocacy (free, independent), the British Heart Foundation’s support for families after a heart attack, cardiac rehabilitation, and NHS Talking Therapies if her symptoms persist.

redFlags: Colin: chest pain not settling after GTN, breathlessness, collapse — 999
Pauline: intrusive replays and insomnia persisting beyond a month, or low mood with hopelessness — reassess and refer
Colin “waiting for the next one”: post-MI depression and anxiety screen needed
psychosocial: She witnessed the arrest and has not slept properly since
Colin withdrawn, not doing his exercises; she fears being widowed
Guilt: two weeks of telling him it was indigestion
ice: Idea: Dr Mensah missed a heart attack and fobbed him off
Concern: the replayed arrest; her own guilt; losing Colin
Expectation: the complaints route today, and to be taken seriously

playbook.diagnosis: Anger carrying two hidden layers: an acute stress reaction after witnessing her husband’s cardiac arrest, and guilt about her own reassurance. The complaint is legitimate and must be handled properly; the clinical work is Colin’s recovery and Pauline’s care.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “What you’re going through — seeing it again and again, not sleeping — is the mind trying to process something terrifying. It usually eases over weeks, and if it doesn’t, there’s treatment that works.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked how to complain, so you have that. And I think underneath there’s a woman who watched her husband nearly die and has been blaming herself ever since.”
management.psychosocial: Complaints route in writing today; Colin’s consent sought for the review to share findings; Colin invited for his own review; Pauline booked in for acute stress follow-up.
sharedPlan: Complaints details today; significant-event review committed; complaint left as her decision
Colin: post-MI review (NICE NG185 drugs, cardiac rehab, mood, DVLA, activity and sex)
Pauline: active monitoring of acute stress (NICE NG116), sleep advice, trauma-focused CBT if symptoms are clinically important or persist
safetyNet: GTN rule: repeat after 5 minutes; 999 if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose
Follow-up call Friday; earlier contact if her mood worsens

pitfalls.intro: Complaint stations are failed through defensiveness, breaches of confidentiality, and stopping at the complaint. The complaint route is the entry ticket; the marks are in the trauma, the guilt and the living patients.

items.fail: Interrupting the opening anger to correct details or explain the colleague’s reasoning.
items.why: “Did not allow the patient to express her concerns.” Arguing with anger escalates it.
items.fix: Two minutes of listening, then: “You asked how to complain, so let me answer that first.”

items.fail: Holding back the complaints route (“let’s see if we can sort it out first”).
items.why: It reads as obstruction, and she has a right to the route.
items.fix: Give it early and completely: practice manager or ICB, timescales, the Ombudsman, the GMC, and details in writing today.

items.fail: Opening Colin’s record and discussing Dr Mensah’s notes with Pauline.
items.why: A confidentiality breach, however sympathetic the listener.
items.fix: “Colin’s records are his. With his permission the review can share everything with you both.”

items.fail: Missing “I’m not doing tears” and the Gaviscon confession.
items.why: “Did not respond to cues.” The trauma and the guilt are the hidden agenda.
items.fix: “You started to tell me what you watched. Would you tell me?” Then meet the guilt with honest context.

items.fail: Ending once the complaint is logged, with no plan for Colin or Pauline.
items.why: The living clinical work (rehab, mood, acute stress) is where Tasks marks sit.
items.fix: Book Colin’s post-MI review and Pauline’s own appointment before the call ends.

items.fail: “Ring 999 if he has chest pain” with no GTN rule and no check.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting in a household five days after an MI.
items.fix: Give the GTN rule and ask her to repeat it back.

The Gaviscon confession: meet it. Then ask how Colin is now and what she fears most.

wordPics.fail: Defends Dr Mensah or agrees she missed it; withholds or delays the complaints route; discusses Colin’s record without his consent; never finds the car park or the Gaviscon; ends with no plan for Colin or for Pauline.
wordPics.pass: Lets her speak, gives the complaints route without defensiveness, commits to a review without judging the colleague, acknowledges her distress, and offers Colin a post-MI review with basic 999 advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: raises Colin’s consent and confidentiality tactfully; returns to the slammed-shut tears; meets the Gaviscon guilt with honest context; recognises her acute stress reaction and books her in; checks the GTN rule by teach-back; dates the follow-up call, and she ends up talking about herself.

avoid.instead: “I wasn’t in that consultation, so I won’t defend or judge it. It will be reviewed properly.”
avoid.why: Reflex defence reads as a closed shop and makes the anger worse.

SCA_MODELS.why: Elicits her current fear and expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: He just sits in the chair, waiting for the next one. Won’t do his exercises. I’m terrified of losing him.

That fear is understandable. Some heart attacks give very little fair warning, and the review will look at what could have been known. The part we can really change now is Colin’s recovery. Cardiac rehab reduces the chance of dying from heart disease by around a fifth to a quarter, and it helps with exactly that fear of the next one.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest context, then turns to secondary prevention

SCA_MODELS.text: He won’t go. He says there’s no point.

Feeling low and frightened after a heart attack is common and treatable. I’d like to see Colin myself this week: his tablets, the rehab, when he can drive, anything he won’t say out loud. Would he come if I rang and invited him?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers Colin a dedicated post-MI review including mood

SCA_MODELS.text: He might, if it came from you.

And you. What you’re describing — the replays, not sleeping — is a normal reaction to something abnormal, and it often settles over a few weeks. I’d like to see you too, and keep an eye on it. If it’s still bad after a month, there is specific therapy that works. I wouldn’t start sleeping tablets.
SCA_MODELS.why: Acute stress reaction: active monitoring, no reflex prescription

SCA_MODELS.text: I suppose I could come in. I didn’t think it was about me.
It is about you as well. So: complaint details to you today, the significant event review, Colin’s appointment, and yours. Does that cover what you need?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises all layers of the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: One more thing for the house. If Colin gets chest pain, he uses his GTN spray. If it isn’t better five minutes after a second dose, or he looks unwell at any point, you ring 999. Could you tell me back what you’d do?
Spray, wait five minutes, spray again, and if it’s not gone five minutes later, 999.
Exactly. I’ll ring you on Friday to see how you both are. Whatever you decide about the complaint, it won’t affect your care.
SCA_MODELS.why: Dated follow-up; complaint left respected as her choice

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. I didn’t expect to end up talking about me.

SCA_STEM.name: Pauline Drake
pmh: Frozen shoulder — seen 10 days ago (Dr Mensah): examination documented, analgesia, physiotherapy referral, safety-net recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Husband Colin, 58, is also registered here: admitted 5 days ago with an inferior MI, stented, now home. Reception note: “VERY unhappy — wants to complain about Dr Mensah, will only speak to a doctor.”
SCA_STEM.reason: Urgent telephone slot requested to make a complaint about another GP.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NHS complaints procedure · GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) · NICE NG185 (acute coronary syndromes, including secondary prevention)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Give the complaints route promptly and without defensiveness, neither defend nor condemn the colleague, respect Colin’s confidentiality, and then turn to the living clinical work: Colin’s recovery, and Pauline as a witness to a cardiac arrest.

points.t: Under the Local Authority Social Services and National Health Service Complaints (England) Regulations 2009, complain to the practice or to the commissioner (the ICB), not both. Acknowledgement within 3 working days, and complaints are normally made within 12 months. If local resolution fails, the next stage is the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. Free NHS complaints advocacy is available. Concerns about a doctor’s fitness to practise can also go straight to the GMC.

The consultation she is complaining about is Colin’s. Anyone complaining on another person’s behalf needs that person’s consent, and his record can’t be discussed with Pauline without it (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). General facts about how heart disease presents are fine to share.

GMC Good Medical Practice: respond to complaints honestly and promptly, and don’t comment unfairly on colleagues. Don’t judge a consultation you weren’t in. Commit to a significant-event analysis, which is appropriate after an MI soon after a consultation. It is fair to say reflux-type symptoms without exertional features can genuinely look like reflux.

NICE NG185: offer cardiac rehabilitation, secondary-prevention drugs, and advice on activity, sex and return to work, and check mood. Cardiac rehabilitation reduces cardiovascular mortality by around a fifth to a quarter. DVLA Group 1: no driving for 1 week after successful PCI, or 4 weeks if not treated by PCI (no need to notify). NICE CG126: GTN, repeat after 5 minutes, and call 999 if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose.

points.h: Pauline: acute stress after a witnessed arrest
points.t: Intrusive replays and insomnia five days after watching her husband’s arrest are an acute stress reaction. NICE NG116: active monitoring and a review within a month; don’t offer psychologically focused debriefing. Consider individual trauma-focused CBT within the first month if she has acute stress disorder or clinically important PTSD symptoms; offer it if they persist beyond a month.

points.h: Guilt: meet it, don’t confirm or dismiss
points.t: “I gave him my Gaviscon” is guilt looking for a target. Explain that burning after meals eased by antacid looks like reflux to anyone; her fortnight isn’t knowable as the cause. Don’t call it “nothing” either: acknowledge how loud it is at 3am.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let the anger run without interrupting or defending; gave the complaints route early because she asked for it.
The witnessed arrest, her sleep, Colin withdrawn at home, fear of being widowed.
“I’m not doing tears”, “she was thorough with ME”, and the Gaviscon confession; each followed up.
Idea (a missed heart attack); concerns (the replayed arrest, her own guilt, losing Colin); expectation (a complaint route today).
Colin: post-MI review (drugs, rehab, mood screen, driving). Pauline: own appointment to assess acute stress and sleep.
Acute stress reaction vs emerging PTSD or depression in Pauline; post-MI anxiety or depression in Colin.
Screened Pauline’s mood and safety; gave household chest-pain and GTN rules with 999 triggers.
Named the anger, trauma and guilt as linked; named acute stress reaction in plain words.
Complaint details in writing today, SEA committed, Colin’s confidentiality respected, both appointments booked, no reflex hypnotic.
Cardiac rehab uptake, secondary prevention, DVLA advice for Colin; sleep and trauma follow-up for Pauline.
GTN rule and 999 triggers checked by teach-back; follow-up call dated; therapy if symptoms persist beyond a month.

social.t: A spouse who witnessed a cardiac arrest, a husband withdrawn after MI, and guilt on both sides. Sleep, work, driving and intimacy are all affected and rarely raised unprompted.

legal.t: Complain to the practice or the ICB; acknowledgement within 3 working days; normally within 12 months; Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman after local resolution. A complaint on someone else’s behalf needs their consent.
GMC Confidentiality (2017): Colin’s consultation details can’t be shared with his wife without his consent, however close they are.
Group 1: stop driving for 1 week after successful PCI (4 weeks if not treated by PCI); no need to notify DVLA. Group 2: 6 weeks and notify.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice: respond promptly, fully and honestly; a complaint must not affect the patient’s care. Don’t make unfair comments about colleagues.
An MI soon after a GP consultation for chest symptoms should be reviewed as a significant event, whether or not anyone complains, with learning shared.
Dr Mensah is entitled to fair process. Neither protecting nor condemning her keeps the review honest.

community.t: NHS complaints advocacy (free, independent), the British Heart Foundation’s support for families after a heart attack, cardiac rehabilitation, and NHS Talking Therapies if her symptoms persist.

redFlags: Colin: chest pain not settling after GTN, breathlessness, collapse — 999
Pauline: intrusive replays and insomnia persisting beyond a month, or low mood with hopelessness — reassess and refer
Colin “waiting for the next one”: post-MI depression and anxiety screen needed
psychosocial: She witnessed the arrest and has not slept properly since
Colin withdrawn, not doing his exercises; she fears being widowed
Guilt: two weeks of telling him it was indigestion
ice: Idea: Dr Mensah missed a heart attack and fobbed him off
Concern: the replayed arrest; her own guilt; losing Colin
Expectation: the complaints route today, and to be taken seriously

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Anger carrying two hidden layers: an acute stress reaction after witnessing her husband’s cardiac arrest, and guilt about her own reassurance. The complaint is legitimate and must be handled properly; the clinical work is Colin’s recovery and Pauline’s care.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “What you’re going through — seeing it again and again, not sleeping — is the mind trying to process something terrifying. It usually eases over weeks, and if it doesn’t, there’s treatment that works.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked how to complain, so you have that. And I think underneath there’s a woman who watched her husband nearly die and has been blaming herself ever since.”
management.psychosocial: Complaints route in writing today; Colin’s consent sought for the review to share findings; Colin invited for his own review; Pauline booked in for acute stress follow-up.
sharedPlan: Complaints details today; significant-event review committed; complaint left as her decision
Colin: post-MI review (NICE NG185 drugs, cardiac rehab, mood, DVLA, activity and sex)
Pauline: active monitoring of acute stress (NICE NG116), sleep advice, trauma-focused CBT if symptoms are clinically important or persist
safetyNet: GTN rule: repeat after 5 minutes; 999 if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose
Follow-up call Friday; earlier contact if her mood worsens

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Complaint stations are failed through defensiveness, breaches of confidentiality, and stopping at the complaint. The complaint route is the entry ticket; the marks are in the trauma, the guilt and the living patients.

items.fail: Interrupting the opening anger to correct details or explain the colleague’s reasoning.
items.why: “Did not allow the patient to express her concerns.” Arguing with anger escalates it.
items.fix: Two minutes of listening, then: “You asked how to complain, so let me answer that first.”

items.fail: Holding back the complaints route (“let’s see if we can sort it out first”).
items.why: It reads as obstruction, and she has a right to the route.
items.fix: Give it early and completely: practice manager or ICB, timescales, the Ombudsman, the GMC, and details in writing today.

items.fail: Opening Colin’s record and discussing Dr Mensah’s notes with Pauline.
items.why: A confidentiality breach, however sympathetic the listener.
items.fix: “Colin’s records are his. With his permission the review can share everything with you both.”

items.fail: Missing “I’m not doing tears” and the Gaviscon confession.
items.why: “Did not respond to cues.” The trauma and the guilt are the hidden agenda.
items.fix: “You started to tell me what you watched. Would you tell me?” Then meet the guilt with honest context.

items.fail: Ending once the complaint is logged, with no plan for Colin or Pauline.
items.why: The living clinical work (rehab, mood, acute stress) is where Tasks marks sit.
items.fix: Book Colin’s post-MI review and Pauline’s own appointment before the call ends.

items.fail: “Ring 999 if he has chest pain” with no GTN rule and no check.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting in a household five days after an MI.
items.fix: Give the GTN rule and ask her to repeat it back.
